content_units: Your symptom combo most strongly points to a   mixture/combustion problem   rather than one isolated part:
-   Intermittent check-engine light   +   rough cold idle   often means a fault that is strongest during cold start, when fuel control is most sensitive.
-   Fuel economy worsening from 7.1 to 8.4 L/100 km   suggests the engine may be running   rich  , misfiring slightly, or correcting for bad air/fuel data.
-   Occasional hesitation in city driving   fits with   misfire, intake leak, dirty throttle body, weak ignition coil, or fuel delivery issues  .
- At   142,000 km  , the most plausible causes are usually in the   ignition, intake/air-metering, or fuel-trim   categories before major internal engine failure.
- Priority:   reliable commuting  , not cosmetic/perfect restoration
- Spark plugs are   not brand new anymore   but also not the first suspect by age alone if they were correctly installed at 110,000 km.
Most Likely Causes and Best First Checks
Likely cause   Why it fits your symptoms   First test to do   Typical repair priority

Ignition coil weakness or intermittent misfire   Rough cold idle, hesitation, flashing/intermittent CEL, poorer fuel economy   Scan for pending/stored misfire codes; misfire counters; coil swap test   Very high
Carbon buildup / dirty throttle body   Cold idle instability, hesitation, airflow disturbance at low speed   Inspect throttle body; idle relearn after cleaning   High
Small vacuum leak / intake leak   Cold idle roughness often worse when cold; lean correction can hurt drivability   Smoke test intake/PCV/hoses/manifold   Very high

MAF/MAP or air-fuel sensor reading drift   Can cause rich/lean fueling and fuel economy drop without constant hard fault   Live data check: fuel trims, MAP/MAF behavior, O2/A/F sensor response   Very high
PCV valve problem   Rough idle, oil vapor issues, poor idle quality, trim problems   Inspect/functional check PCV system   Medium-high
Fuel injector imbalance or deposit buildup   Rough idle, city hesitation, mileage loss   Misfire/fuel trim review; injector balance or contribution testing   Medium-high

Early catalytic converter inefficiency caused by prolonged misfire/rich running   Can trigger CEL and worsen performance after root cause persists   Only evaluate after misfire/fueling checks   Medium
Diagnostic Order That Makes the Most Sense
A good mechanic should   not start by replacing random parts  . The smartest first-hour approach is:
1) Pull codes and live data first
-   Stored, pending, and history OBD-II codes
-   A/F sensor and O2 sensor behavior
- An intermittent CEL usually leaves   clues even when the light is off  .
- This may immediately separate   misfire  ,   lean condition  ,   rich condition  , or   sensor plausibility  .
- A small leak can create   cold rough idle + hesitation + trim issues   and is often cheaper to fix than sensors.
- Swap suspect coils cylinder-to-cylinder if misfire follows
- Verify plugs are correct type and gap if needed
- A weak coil is a very plausible cause and can be fixed within budget.
4) Inspect and clean throttle body; perform idle relearn
- Hondas can develop   idle quality issues   when the throttle body gets dirty.
- This is relatively low-cost and often helps with   cold idle and tip-in hesitation  .
5) Evaluate MAP/air-fuel sensor data before replacing sensors
- Sensor values are plausible at idle and under light load
- Fuel trims indicate   lean correction   or   rich correction
- Sensor replacement can get expensive fast; verify before buying parts.
6) Fuel injector / fuel pressure testing if earlier steps don’t solve it
- Less commonly the first thing to fail than leaks/coils/throttle-body issues, but still plausible.
Most Cost-Effective Repair Sequence for a 900 CAD Budget
1.   Diagnostic scan with live data + freeze frame
3.   Ignition diagnosis focused on coils/misfire source
6.   Targeted sensor replacement only if data proves it
7.   Injector or catalyst work only after root cause confirmed
A realistic commuting-first plan would be:
- repairing a split hose or intake leak
- replace   only the failed coil   first, or a small set if clearly justified
-   Step D: If sensor data is clearly bad
This sequence gives you the best chance of staying under   900 CAD   without wasting money.
Minor intake leak, dirty throttle body, or weak ignition coil
- Best fit for all symptoms together
- Highest likelihood of restoring commuter reliability quickly
- Can produce rough idle and economy drop
- Usually not the first blind replacement item, but worth checking early
Less likely as the starting point
- Possible, but not the first bet unless there are signs like:
- Scan for   stored, pending, and history codes
- Print or report   freeze-frame and fuel trims
- Do a   smoke test for intake/vacuum leaks
- Inspect   coils, plug wells, and plug condition
- Inspect/clean   throttle body   and perform   idle relearn
- Replace parts   only after confirming the failed circuit/component
That wording helps prevent a “parts cannon” approach.
